contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Do not outline unknown categories. Leave a plain gap, or switch to an open form such as a row of labelled category pips that appear only when known. For T1, draw only the categories a saved place can hold. Before committing, test the ring with 5 pilot users by asking 'what does this tell you?' and check whether anyone says 'almost done'.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: Each species is drawn in four moods, 'relaxed, attentive, fidgeting, worried', and 'Worried — "A bill is overdue."' is a distinct distressed-sounding pose.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: In Fish'n'Steps, some participants ignored the display when their fish was unhappy, and the reported reading is that punishment led to avoidance (as reported in Consolvo et al. 2008). UbiFit deliberately used only positive reinforcement. Duolingo's sad-owl messaging is the leading example of guilt-based engagement.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Keep four states, but define the top two as helpful urgency, not distress: 'busy', with the keeper holding a stack, and 'needs you', with the keeper holding up the envelope or pointing at the line. Never draw tears, cowering or illness. Rename the internal states so illustrators don't draw anxiety, and add an 'Already paid?' correction on the overdue line.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: State 6: after Skip, 'Today drawn with the quiet inline invitation still in the keeper slot'. The keeper-strip prompt likewise keeps an 'Unnamed' invitation in place, even though the naming prompt says Skip 'never asks again'.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: Apple's HIG on onboarding says not to present a skipped flow again on later launches and to make it findable in settings or help. Deceptive.design classes 'Not now' without a permanent dismissal as nagging. The European Parliament's 2023 resolution calls for attention-seeking features to be off by design.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: After Skip, the keeper slot on Today closes entirely and Today looks the way it does for a user who has no keeper. Re-entry is a row in the place file's Place section and a Settings item. Update the Skipped frame and the strip's Unnamed frame to match.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: The receipt row reads 'Ollie, your keeper - knows 11 things about this address' (and x-place-file's entry point is 'See what we know').
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: The keeper-strip prompt itself forbids 'a "knows 11 things" growth game'. Tying a count to the keeper links the creature's identity to data quantity, which is the quantification pattern Etkin 2016 associates with lower enjoyment. 'Knows' also frames data-holding as surveillance, since people see data-driven tailoring as useful and invasive at once (Ur et al. 2012; weak, by analogy).
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Split the row: 'Ollie (your keeper)' as one carried item, and '11 things on file' as a separate row, or drop the count. Rename 'See what we know' to 'See your place file'.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: The Founding Neighbor tier is 'a warning-tinted countdown pill … reading "closes in 6 days"' plus 'a thin 21-day depletion bar'.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: The deadline is real, so this is not a deceptive timer. But Mathur et al. 2019 and the FTC 2022 report put countdown and limited-time framing in the urgency category, and Apple's HIG asks that urgency be represented accurately. The sibling prompt f9-founding-meter-preview chose 'a date, not a live countdown number', and elsewhere in the product warning tokens mark consequential obligations such as voter registration.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Use a neutral or info pill with the date ('Closes Tue, Sep 22') and draw the depletion bar in neutral tokens. Keep the fail-closed rule, and keep rank and tier as visibly different shapes.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: All locked tiers are listed with remaining counts, including '10 neighbors join … 7 more neighbors who join' and '25 neighbors join … 22 more neighbors who join', in a 30-person pilot.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: Effort follows the proportion of the goal remaining (Kivetz et al. 2006), so distant tiers pull little and mostly record a shortfall. Badges and social comparison lowered motivation over time (Hanus & Fox 2015). UbiFit added alternate goals to keep goals reachable. The prompt already recognises that 'a 0/1/0/0 tier list is demoralising'.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Show the unlocked tiers, the next locked tier with its count, and collapse the rest into 'More rewards (2)'. Keep the payload-driven rows so tiers can be added without layout changes.

numbers: Silverman & Barasch (JCR 2022/23): 7 studies. Strength-exercise study continuation was 66.23% with an intact streak vs 57.86% with a broken one, for identical behaviour (INSEAD Knowledge).
Nunes & Drèze (JCR 2006): a 10-stamp card with 2 pre-filled stamps was completed by 34%, vs 19% for a plain 8-stamp card, for the same 8 purchases.

Consolvo et al. 2008: 28 participants over 3 months. The glanceable display maintained activity, and it dropped significantly without the display. Weekly goals. Up to 3 small butterflies for recent goal attainment.
Consolvo et al. 2009: default goal week Monday–Sunday. Daily goals were unappealing because people need rest days. For less active users, a 4-week window was suggested.
Fish'n'Steps (Lin et al. 2006): 19 participants. Some ignored the display when the fish was unhappy.
watchOS 11 ring pause: today, this week, this month, or a custom 1–90 days, with the streak kept.

Duolingo blog: streak milestone animation +1.7% D7 retention for new learners. Two equipped Streak Freezes +0.38% daily active learners. Company claim: users who reach a 7-day streak are 3.6x more likely to complete their course.
Duolingo KDD 2020 notification bandit: +0.5% DAU, +2.0% new-user D7 retention. Repeating the same template desensitises users.
PLOS One run-streak study: 17 runners, all of whom ended streaks of 100 or more consecutive days. Some ran injured, and some grieved for weeks to months.
Diefenbach & Müssig (IJHCS 2019): 45 Habitica users over 2 weeks. All experienced counterproductive effects.
Sailer & Homner meta-analysis (2020): gamification effects g = .49 cognitive, .36 motivational, .25 behavioural, with motivational and behavioural effects less stable in rigorous studies.
Etkin (JCR 2016): six experiments. Measurement increases output but reduces enjoyment.

Chernev et al. choice-overload meta-analysis: 99 observations, N = 7,202. Overload rises with task difficulty, complexity, preference uncertainty and an effort-minimising goal. Keep keeper species at 6 or fewer, with no sub-choices.
Finch first run (Revyl Atlas): 45 screens, a 6-colour egg picker, and a pre-filled random pet name. The Pantopus target is one sheet.
Mathur et al. 2019: about 53K product pages on about 11K sites. 1,818 dark-pattern instances across 15 types and 7 categories, and 183 sites with deceptive practices.
WCAG 2.2.2 (Level A): auto-starting motion that lasts more than 5 seconds alongside other content needs pause, stop or hide. Keep keeper idle loops at 5 seconds or less, or no loop.
WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA): interaction-triggered motion can be disabled. Honour prefers-reduced-motion and Reduce Motion with a static pose.
Apple Time Sensitive interruption level: only for events happening now or within an hour. Never use it for keeper or mood content.
European Parliament resolution on addictive design adopted 12 December 2023. It calls for a 'right not to be disturbed', with attention-seeking features off by design.
Keeper name limit 24 characters (v1 prompt). The mood horizon should be worded 'next 7 days' (rolling) rather than a calendar week that resets. This is a recommendation, not a sourced figure.

Not verified, do not cite: Headspace's streak and companion practices (I found no primary source), the Material 3 'Design Principles for Digital Wellbeing' page (it renders client-side and I could not read it), '63% more likely to abandon after one missed day', and 'CHI 2020 streak anxiety' (blog claims with no primary source found).

topic: capture-and-extraction: photographing paper mail and bills, reviewing what the machine read, mail triage, and the privacy of stored document photos (f10-mail-day-triage, f10-snap-capture-tray, f10-extraction-confirm, f10-mail-piece-photo, f10-bill-provenance, f10-bill-trend, f10-mail-snap-privacy)

principles.principle: Capture with the platform's document scanner, not a plain camera. Pantopus owns what happens after capture, not the viewfinder.
principles.evidence: ML Kit Document Scanner (Android): 'Automatic capture with document detection', 'Accurate edge detection for optimal crop results', crop, rotate, reorder and filters. It runs entirely on the device, and 'No camera permission is required'. It needs Android API 21+ and at least 1.7 GB RAM (below that it throws an MlKitException). Its UI 'is provided by the SDK': you can only set gallery import, a page limit and the scanner mode. Apple VNDocumentCameraViewController 'presents UI for a camera pass-through that helps people scan physical documents... page by page' and returns 'images, by page number'. isSupported 'returns false for unsupported hardware'. A secondary tutorial (Scanbot, not fetched: DNS failure) says it offers no page limit, no reordering and no custom strings. Apple Notes, which uses the same scanner, defaults to Auto mode, lets you drag the corners, then 'Keep Scan', add more pages, then Done.
principles.implication: Stop drawing a custom Pantopus viewfinder with a strip inside it. Neither system scanner accepts custom chrome. A plain system camera picker takes one shot and has no edge detection. Split the tray into two stages. (1) The system scanner session (VNDocumentCameraViewController on iOS, GmsDocumentScanner in SCANNER_MODE_BASE on Android) handles auto-capture, edges, retake and multi-page. (2) The Pantopus 'capture tray' is the upload queue that opens when the scanner returns: thumbnails, per-file progress, delete, retry, the audience line, 'Scan more' (reopens the scanner and appends) and 'Done'. Draw two fallback frames: 'scanner not supported on this device' (iOS isSupported false, Android RAM below 1.7 GB), which falls back to the photo picker or a single camera shot, and 'camera permission denied' (iOS and web only, because Android's scanner needs no permission).

principles.principle: Auto-capture should be the default but reversible, and a manual shutter must always be visible. Never let a custom camera fire on its own with no manual option.
principles.evidence: Apple Notes scanner: in Auto mode 'your document will automatically scan'. For manual capture, 'tap the Shutter button or press one of the Volume buttons'. An Apple Community thread asks for Manual to be the default and finds no such setting. The user calls toggling before the scanner auto-fires burdensome. Genius Scan: 'Genius Scan will detect it automatically', shows an orange overlay when it sees a document, and lets users turn auto-capture off in Settings for more time to position the page.
principles.implication: With system scanners the Auto/Manual switch is the system's, so do not re-draw it. In any fallback camera Pantopus draws (web mobile, unsupported devices), show a large manual shutter and never auto-fire. Detection feedback (an outline when a page is found) belongs in the viewfinder, not in a banner.

principles.principle: Scanning is batch-first: the camera stays open, a page counter grows, and finishing is a deliberate act. Pages and mail pieces are different things, and the tray must let people group them.
principles.evidence: Genius Scan: 'Genius Scan is in Batch mode by default so you can keep scanning documents to create a multipage document'. A counter shows the pages captured, and a checkmark ends the batch. After a page is validated, the user returns to the camera rather than being asked to add another. A later release (changelog, search result only) added a screen to review all captured pages with bulk delete and reordering. Apple Notes: 'tap the Done button or add additional scans'. Search-result summaries of user reviews (not verified first-hand) say Microsoft Lens allowed no reordering of batch pages before export. Microsoft retired Lens in January 2026 (backend off March 9, 2026; support page, search result only).
principles.implication: v1 is right to make batch the default. The gap: a 2-page Clark PUD bill scanned in one session comes back as two images, and v1 treats every shot as one piece ('Piece 3 of 5'). Default to one page = one piece. Give each thumbnail after the first a visible 'Same letter as previous' join control, and show a joined piece as a stacked thumbnail with a page count ('2 pages'). The confirm screen's counter counts pieces, not photos.

principles.principle: A model's confidence is not correctness. Tie every extracted value to where it was read on the page, including the printed label it sat beside.
principles.evidence: Nutrient: 'model certainty and extraction correctness aren't the same thing'. Its example returned $6,500 with 97% confidence from the wrong table column. Microsoft Content Understanding uses a scanned utility bill as its example: billing address at confidence 0.96, amount due at 0.52. Grounding gives the page number and bounding-box coordinates for 'efficient human-in-the-loop validation'. In the peer-reviewed Bias in the Loop study (N=2,784), reviewers corrected digit-swap errors 82% of the time, and values present on the page but in the wrong cell (a different year or scope) about 77% of the time. Errors that required understanding the rules were corrected only 31% of the time.
principles.implication: On f10-extraction-confirm, give Amount and Due date a caption naming the label they were read from ('Read beside "Amount due"', 'Read beside "Due date"'). On a bill, the typical miss is 'Previous balance' vs 'Amount due', or 'Statement date' vs 'Due date', and a high score hides exactly that. v1 already zooms to the region when a field is tapped. When no region exists, say so in words ('We can't point to where we read this') rather than only leaving the pane un-outlined.

principles.principle: Make checking cheaper than trusting. Explanations reduce over-reliance only when they lower the cost of checking.
principles.evidence: Vasconcelos et al., CSCW 2023, 'Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making': people weigh the cost of checking against the benefit of relying on the AI. The authors suggest some null results in the literature arise because 'the explanation not sufficiently reducing the costs of verifying the AI's prediction'. Vendor HITL guides describe the same mechanism: LandingAI shows the value, its score and the source region side by side, and reports a 40–60% cut in review time at one bank (vendor claim). Mindee has reviewers 'click a data field and verify the source in seconds'.
principles.implication: Keep v1's pinned photo beside the fields, and shorten the distance further. When a field is focused, put a cropped snippet of its source region directly above the value (the row shows the printed '$184.62' crop, then the editable $184.62), so the check is two things one line apart, not a glance up to a pane 300 pt away. Draw amount and due date at body/h3 size, not caption.

principles.principle: Every added step on the correction path lowers the number of corrections. Editing a wrong value must be the lowest-effort path on the screen.
principles.evidence: Bias in the Loop (randomised, N=2,784): 'requiring corrections for pre-annotations annotated as incorrect resulted in significantly fewer corrections, more undercorrections, and fewer overcorrections'. Accuracy was only slightly higher (68% vs 66%, p=0.028). The authors report 'a weak tendency for annotators to reduce their workload by underreporting errors'. Financial incentives had no effect.
principles.implication: A tap on any field opens the right control in place (decimal pad with the value selected, native date picker), with no 'What's wrong?' reason picker or separate 'Report' flow. Reserve the provenance sheet's 'This isn't right' for public-record facts, not for photo reads. Keep the per-piece field set to what changes behaviour: payee, amount, due date. Collapse 'Account ending' and 'Kind' into a secondary row so a 5-piece stack stays short.

principles.principle: Glancing to compare a pre-filled value with a photo is a weak check. Help the eye for the one value that costs money.
principles.evidence: Barchard's lab (UNLV Interactive Measurement Group), summarising their data-entry experiments: 'Visual checking was no more accurate than single entry: Both resulted in roughly 30 times as many errors as double entry.' Barchard & Pace (2011), Computers in Human Behavior 27, reports the original study (195 participants; abstract seen only via search).
principles.implication: Don't make people retype the amount: the principle above says added effort suppresses corrections. Instead, (a) put the source crop next to the amount (see the principle on cheaper checking), (b) put the values in the commit button itself, 'Add $184.62 due Oct 2 to bills', so the last thing read before committing is the value, and (c) state the amount again in the success line: 'Added $184.62 to your calendar. We'll remind you 7 days before.'

principles.principle: Show uncertainty per field, in plain words, where it matters. No numeric scores for consumers, and no generic 'AI can be wrong' banner as the only cue.
principles.evidence: Google PAIR: if confidence 'doesn't make an impact on user decision making, consider not showing it'. Numeric displays assume users understand probability. Categorical buckets or N-best alternatives suit lay users. NN/g: move 'beyond generic disclaimers that become background clutter' and show warnings 'at moments when it is more likely to be relevant'. It also suggests first-person uncertainty language. Box Preview flags low-confidence fields 'directly in the metadata panel next to the corresponding metadata value'. Frontiers (N=93): an instruction warning of system errors increased checking (d=0.67) but did not significantly improve correct decisions.
principles.implication: Keep v1's ban on percentages. An uncertain field gets a text flag in the row as well as a shape ('We weren't sure — check this'), so the cue survives screen readers and small sizes. When the model found two candidate dates, offer them as two tappable options ('Oct 2' / 'Oct 12', from 'Due date' and 'Statement date') rather than silently picking one. Drop any screen-level 'AI-generated' banner.

principles.principle: Once a person has accepted or edited a value, clear the machine's uncertainty from it. The record says what the person did, not what the model doubted.
principles.evidence: Box Preview: Accept 'Confirms the extracted value is correct. The field is marked "Accepted", the confidence flag is cleared.' Edit 'Requires the user to enter the correct value. The field is marked "Edited," and both the confidence level and bounding box are removed.' Microsoft Content Understanding: after correction, 'corrected fields display the corrected tag'.
principles.implication: On f10-bill-provenance every committed bill carries the filled-with-tick mark. A history line may say 'We read Oct 2; you changed it to Oct 12 on Oct 3', but the mark never reverts to hollow. The same applies to the f10-bill-trend column mark and the Today strip.

principles.principle: When extraction fails, fields must look empty, never hold a plausible default. Preserve anything the person typed.
principles.evidence: Expensify fixed a bug where 'When a receipt fails to scan, the Amount field showed "$0.00" with no error instead of staying empty'. After the fix the field stays blank with a 'missing amount' error until the user enters a value. NN/g error-message guidelines: be specific, 'offer constructive advice', 'Preserve the user's input', and avoid blame words such as invalid or incorrect.
principles.implication: In the 'AI unavailable' and 'unreadable photo' frames, draw fields with placeholders ('Amount', 'Due date') and no value, never $0.00 or today's date. Add inline 'Needed to add a bill' on Amount and Due date only when the user presses 'Add to bills'. 'Just file it' needs no fields. The error frame keeps every typed value, as v1 already says.

principles.principle: Nothing the machine read reaches money, calendar or reminders until a person commits it, and every commit is checked, confirmed or reversible. Suggestions learn only from confirmed data.
principles.evidence: WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data): for actions with financial effects, or that modify or delete user data, the action must be 'Reversible, Checked, or Confirmed'. A search result from the Paperless-ngx docs (first-hand fetch returned 403) says its Auto matching 'only takes documents into account which are NOT placed in your inbox', so it learns only from documents already reviewed. Search summaries of Expensify community threads (not verified first-hand) describe misread amounts being approved when nothing flagged them.
principles.implication: 'Add to bills' restates the values (see the principle on visual checking) and is followed by an Undo. The 'recent payee' suggestions on the Payee field come only from bills the household has committed, never from unconfirmed reads. Unconfirmed amounts never appear in f10-bill-trend or in any nearby average.

principles.principle: Triage keeps each piece in one visible 'needs a call' state until a person decides. What happens to the paper and to the scan are decided together, and the list never claims to be complete.
principles.evidence: Paperless-ngx: new documents get an inbox tag, and the recommended workflow ends with 'remove inbox tags from the documents' after assigning a correspondent, a type and checking the date. It also warns that date reading 'fails sometimes if the OCR is bad or multiple dates appear'. Earth Class Mail (help-centre search results; direct fetch returned 403) pairs the physical outcome with the scan's fate: 'Recycle and Keep Scan', 'Recycle and Move Scan to Archive', 'Recycle and Move Scan to Trash'. USPS Informed Delivery shows 'grayscale images' of the address side, usually by 9 AM, and notes that 'Not every item appears in the preview... A piece can still arrive even if it does not show up.'
principles.implication: Mail Day rows stay in 'Needs a call' until decided. The trailing decision for a photographed piece offers the paper decision and the photo decision in one control ('Recycled · keep photo' / 'Recycled · delete photo'). Copy says 'the mail you've added today', never 'all of today's mail'.

principles.principle: Ask for camera access only at the moment of capture, with a specific purpose sentence. Prefer pickers that need no permission for the fallback.
principles.evidence: Apple HIG Privacy: 'Request access only to data that you actually need'. Ideally wait 'until people actually use an app feature that requires access'. Purpose strings should be 'a brief, complete sentence that's straightforward, specific'. A pre-alert screen should 'Include only one button', titled 'Continue' or 'Next', with no cancel or close. Android Photo Picker needs no runtime permission, runs on Android 11+ (backported to 4.4 via Play services) and caps multi-select at getPickImagesMaxLimit(). ML Kit's scanner needs no camera permission. VisionKit's DataScannerViewController documents the NSCameraUsageDescription requirement.
principles.implication: The tray's 'camera permission denied' frame applies to iOS and web. Its fallback 'Choose from photos instead' opens PHPicker or Android Photo Picker, which ask for no library permission, so the copy must not ask for photo access. If a pre-permission screen is drawn, it has one 'Continue' button and names the purpose ('to photograph bills and letters you choose to add to your home'). Run the claimed-home and finance checks before any permission prompt, as v1 already says.

principles.principle: Keep as little of a document photo as the job needs, for as short a time as it needs. Account numbers are the first thing to minimise.
principles.evidence: FTC, 'Protecting Personal Information': 'Keep only what you need for your business'. Don't keep customer credit card information 'unless you have a business need for it'. Keep a written retention policy stating 'how long to keep it, and how to dispose of it'. GDPR Art. 25(2), privacy by default, requires that by default 'only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose' are processed, explicitly including 'the period of their storage'. Apple HIG: 'Process data on the device where possible.'
principles.implication: Store and show only the account's last 4 digits, and never offer a field for the full number. Give the stored photo a stated, bounded retention by default, so the privacy card's count line reads like '17 photos · 41.3 MB · kept 90 days, then deleted' (90 is a placeholder for a product decision, not a sourced number). Keep 'Delete all' on the card, and let 'Delete this photo' on the piece leave the amounts in place.

principles.principle: Name exactly who can see a document photo, including people inside the household, and keep the statement accurate when permissions differ.
principles.evidence: Zeng & Roesner (USENIX Security 2019), multi-user smart homes: technology 'is often not well designed for multiple users, sometimes lacking basic access control', and tensions arise 'even in well-functioning, non-adversarial households'. Their prototype added access controls and activity notifications. Apple HIG: 'Be transparent about how your app collects and uses people's data.'
principles.implication: The always-visible tray line names the audience: 'Only your household can see these photos: you and Sam.' The privacy card must not say 'Everyone in this household can see them' when a member without finance.view cannot open bill photos (as f10-mail-piece-photo specifies). Name the difference instead: 'Sam sees that a bill arrived, not the photo or the amount.'

principles.principle: Destructive actions state exactly what goes and what stays, use buttons that describe the outcome, and use undo rather than a confirm for low-stakes deletes.
principles.evidence: NN/g: use confirmation dialogs for serious consequences only. 'Do not use confirmation dialogs for routine actions'. 'Do not ask Are you sure'. Provide 'response options that summarize what will happen'. 'Avoid giving confirmation dialogs a default Yes answer'. 'Do go to great lengths to provide undo'. WCAG 3.3.4 accepts Reversible or Confirmed for data deletion.
principles.implication: v1's named-survivor confirms are right: keep them for 'Delete this photo', 'Delete the bill and the photo' and 'Delete all 17 photos'. Deleting a shot in the capture tray, before upload, gets no dialog: remove it immediately with an 'Undo' on the strip. Neither confirm button carries default focus.

principles.principle: Controls on small thumbnails still need full-size hit areas, and a gesture is never the only way to do something important.
principles.evidence: Apple HIG Buttons: 'a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt'. Apple HIG Gestures: a custom gesture must be 'Not the only way to perform an important action'. Android: 'touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp'. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8: targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or spaced so 24 px circles don't intersect.
principles.implication: On the tray strip, tapping a thumbnail selects it and shows a visible action row ('Retake' · 'Delete' · 'Same letter as previous') at 44 pt / 48 dp. Long-press and hover may be shortcuts only. The per-file progress ring must not sit under the delete target.

principles.principle: An undo that expires is a time limit, and the person must be able to extend it or it must last a long time.
principles.evidence: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable: for each time limit set by content, the user can turn it off, adjust it to at least ten times the default, or be warned and given 'at least 20 seconds to extend' it. Exceptions are real-time, essential, or limits longer than 20 hours.
principles.implication: On Mail Day, per-row Undo on 'Reviewed today' stays available until the day is finished, which also covers the over-20-hours exception. Drop the '(4s)' countdown. A snackbar may echo the action, but it is not the only way back.

principles.principle: Web capture is a file picker with a camera hint, not a viewfinder, and iPhone photo formats don't display in most browsers.
principles.evidence: MDN, capture attribute: 'these work better on mobile devices; if your device is a desktop computer, you'll likely get a typical file picker'. It is 'not Baseline'. caniuse: HEIF/HEIC displays only in Safari 17+; Chrome, Firefox and Edge have no support.
principles.implication: The web tray draws a drop target and a 'Choose files' button, never viewfinder chrome, as v1 already does for desktop. Mobile web gets 'Take a photo' (capture=environment) plus 'Choose from library'. Convert HEIC to JPEG before drawing thumbnails or opening the piece viewer on web, or Chrome users see broken images.

patterns.name: System scanner session plus app-owned upload queue
patterns.exemplars: Apple Notes and Files use VNDocumentCameraViewController (auto-capture, corner drag, Keep Scan / Retake, add pages, Done). Android apps such as Google Drive use the ML Kit GmsDocumentScanner (auto-capture, edge detection, crop, rotate, reorder, on-device, no camera permission). Genius Scan defaults to batch, shows a page counter and returns to the camera after each page.
patterns.howToApply: Mail Day's 'Scan today's stack' launches the system scanner. When it returns N images, Pantopus shows the tray over Mail Day: a thumbnail per page with an upload ring, delete, retake (reopens the scanner for one page), 'Same letter as previous', the household audience line, 'Scan more' and 'Done (N)'. Extraction runs in the background, so people shoot the whole stack now and confirm later.
patterns.pitfalls: Neither scanner can be customised, so Pantopus text cannot go inside the viewfinder. ML Kit needs at least 1.7 GB RAM, and VisionKit has isSupported, so a fallback is required. Pages are not pieces, so grouping is needed. Request JPEG from ML Kit (setResultFormats), not PDF, if the backend accepts images only.

patterns.name: Source-grounded field review (tap a field, jump to its region)
patterns.exemplars: Microsoft Content Understanding returns a confidence score and grounding (page plus bounding box) for every field, for jumping 'directly to the source'. Mindee has reviewers 'click a data field and verify the source in seconds' using polygons. LandingAI shows value, score and source region side by side.
patterns.howToApply: f10-extraction-confirm: the pinned photo (phone) or left pane (desktop) zooms to and outlines the region when a field gets focus. Add an inline crop of that region inside the focused row and a caption naming the printed label read ('beside "Amount due"').
patterns.pitfalls: LLM image extraction (the design doc's input_image approach) may return no coordinates. Never invent a box. Say 'We can't point to where we read this' and leave the pane at fit-to-width. Grounding shows where a value came from, not that it is the right value, so the wrong-column case still needs the label caption.

patterns.name: Per-field accept/edit that clears the flag
patterns.exemplars: Box Preview: Accept marks a field 'Accepted' and clears the confidence flag. Edit marks it 'Edited' and removes the confidence level and bounding box. Microsoft Content Understanding Studio tags corrected fields 'corrected'.
patterns.howToApply: On confirm, uncertain fields carry a text flag until touched. Editing one clears the flag and records 'You changed this'. Committing turns the whole piece to filled-with-tick. f10-bill-provenance shows the history ('We read Oct 2; you changed it to Oct 12') without reverting to hollow.
patterns.pitfalls: Requiring an explicit per-field 'Accept' tap on every field adds effort, which lowers corrections (Bias in the Loop). Limit mandatory attention to uncertain fields and let the commit button carry the rest.

patterns.name: Offer the alternatives the model found instead of hiding them
patterns.exemplars: Google PAIR lists 'N-best alternatives' as a way to express uncertainty that helps users apply their own judgment. Paperless-ngx warns that date reading 'fails sometimes if the OCR is bad or multiple dates appear'.
patterns.howToApply: When a bill shows several dates (statement date, due date, service period), the Due date row shows the model's pick plus one or two tappable alternatives, each with its printed label: 'Oct 2 (Due date)' · 'Sep 12 (Statement date)'.
patterns.pitfalls: More than 3 options turns a check into a hunt. Show alternatives only when the extractor actually returned them, and never pad the list.

patterns.name: Blank-not-zero when the read fails
patterns.exemplars: Expensify changed a failed SmartScan from showing '$0.00' to leaving Amount blank with a 'missing amount' error until the user enters a value (PR 98871).
patterns.howToApply: The 'AI unavailable' and 'unreadable photo' frames on f10-extraction-confirm show placeholders only. 'Just file it' stays enabled. 'Add to bills' asks for Amount and Due date inline only after it is pressed.
patterns.pitfalls: Don't let the date control default to today or the amount pad to 0.00. Either becomes a real bill if the user taps through.

patterns.name: Inbox-until-reviewed triage with paired paper/scan disposition
patterns.exemplars: Paperless-ngx puts an inbox tag on every new document, and review ends by removing it. Earth Class Mail (help centre) offers 'Recycle and Keep Scan / Move Scan to Archive / Move Scan to Trash'. USPS Informed Delivery gives a grayscale preview per piece and says not every piece appears.
patterns.howToApply: Mail Day rows remain in 'Needs a call' until decided. A photographed piece's decision control records the paper outcome and the photo outcome together. The Reviewed list keeps per-row undo until 'Finish day'. Copy never claims completeness.
patterns.pitfalls: Don't add a completion meter (v1 already forbids one). Don't let 'Recycled' silently keep a bank-statement photo forever. The photo outcome is part of the decision.

patterns.name: Permission-free fallback pickers
patterns.exemplars: Android Photo Picker needs no runtime permission (Android 11+, backported to 4.4 via Play services). iOS PHPicker (per Apple's WWDC20 limited-library guidance, search result only) lets people pick photos without granting library access.
patterns.howToApply: 'Choose from photos instead' in the tray's permission-denied and scanner-unsupported frames opens the system picker with multi-select and never shows a library-permission prompt.
patterns.pitfalls: Android's picker caps selection (getPickImagesMaxLimit()). Show the cap in the picker's calling copy if a stack could exceed it.

patterns.name: Consequence-naming destructive confirms, undo for cheap deletes
patterns.exemplars: NN/g confirmation-dialog guidance: specific consequences, outcome-describing buttons, no default Yes, and undo wherever possible.
patterns.howToApply: Keep v1's confirms that name what survives ('The bill and its amount stay; only the photo is removed'), with buttons 'Delete 17 photos' / 'Keep them'. Tray shot deletion before upload is instant with Undo, no dialog.
patterns.pitfalls: A confirm dialog on every thumbnail delete trains people to tap through, which weakens the confirm on the dangerous 'Delete all'.

antipatterns: A confidence percentage, meter or single document-level score on consumer extraction fields. PAIR says numeric confidence assumes users understand probability and adds nothing when it doesn't change a decision, and Nutrient shows a 97% score on a wrong-column value.

Using Pantopus's FILLED shape ('official or confirmed', per x-provenance-sheet) for a value a model read from the user's own photo. A machine read of a snapshot is neither a published record nor user-confirmed, and a 'done' look invites skipping the check (automation bias; Bias in the Loop).

A generic 'AI can make mistakes' banner as the only uncertainty cue. NN/g says generic disclaimers become background clutter, and in the Frontiers study an error-awareness instruction raised checking effort without significantly improving correct decisions.
Pre-filling $0.00, today's date or a guessed payee when extraction fails. Expensify had to fix exactly this, because a plausible default becomes a real bill when someone taps through.

A reason picker, a separate 'report' flow or any extra step before a user can correct a field. Adding effort to correction produced fewer corrections and more missed errors in a randomised study of 2,784 people.
A one-shot camera picker that dismisses after every photo. System scanners and Genius Scan keep the camera open, count pages and make finishing deliberate.
Drawing a custom Pantopus viewfinder on top of VisionKit or ML Kit scanners. Their UI cannot be customised, so the design cannot ship as drawn.

Long-press or hover as the only way to retake or delete a shot, or delete glyphs with hit areas under 44 pt / 48 dp. Apple HIG says a custom gesture must not be the only way to perform an important action, and Apple, Android and WCAG 2.5.8 set minimum target sizes.
A self-firing capture in any camera Pantopus draws itself, with no manual shutter. Apple Notes users complain they cannot make Manual the default.
A 4-second countdown as the only way to undo a triage decision. WCAG 2.2.1 requires a time limit to be adjustable or extendable, or to exceed 20 hours.

Keeping document photos indefinitely by default, or storing or showing more than an account's last 4 digits. FTC says keep only what you need, and GDPR Art. 25(2) requires privacy by default for the storage period.

A privacy line that says only 'private to your home' or 'never shown to neighbors' without naming who inside the household can see a photographed bank statement, or one that says 'everyone in the household' when finance permissions differ. Zeng & Roesner found real tensions inside households.
Copy that implies Mail Day holds all of today's mail ('Inbox zero', 'All caught up on your mail'). Even USPS Informed Delivery says not every piece appears.
Learning payee suggestions or amount patterns from unconfirmed reads. Paperless-ngx learns only from documents already reviewed.
'Are you sure?' confirms with Yes/No buttons, or a default-focused destructive button (NN/g).
Rendering HEIC thumbnails directly on web. Only Safari 17+ can display them, so Chrome, Firefox and Edge users see broken images.
Promising a live viewfinder on desktop web. MDN says the capture attribute falls back to a file picker on desktop and is not Baseline.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: 'Confidence is expressed PER FIELD and only as the system's provenance marks: a hollow mark beside Due date and Account ending, a filled mark on the confident fields.' Payee, Amount and Kind are drawn with the filled mark before the user has confirmed anything.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: In the shared encoding (x-provenance-sheet), FILLED means 'official or confirmed'. Before commit, no field is either. Model confidence is not correctness: Nutrient shows a wrong-column value at 97%, and Microsoft's own utility-bill example has amount due at 0.52 while the address is 0.96, so the money field is often the weak one. Reviewers accept wrong values readily (Bias in the Loop). Marking fields as settled lowers checking of exactly the values that cost money, and it breaks house honesty rule 1 (unverified must look unverified).
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Before commit, every extracted field carries the hollow 'read, not yet confirmed' treatment (or a fourth 'read from your photo' variant defined once in x-provenance-sheet). Uncertain fields add a text flag, 'We weren't sure — check this', with alternatives where the model found them. Amount and Due date always get the source crop and the 'read beside "…"' caption whatever the model's confidence. On 'Add to bills' the whole piece becomes filled-with-tick.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: State 3, 'Low-confidence extraction': 'the mark stays hollow and one extra line appears: "We weren't sure about the due date. You changed it on Oct 3."'
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: Once a person accepts or edits a value, review tools clear the machine's flag: Box marks it Accepted or Edited and removes the confidence and bounding box, and Microsoft tags it 'corrected'. v1's own extraction screen says nothing reaches bills before the user confirms it, so a bill with a hollow mark would claim a confirmed fact is unconfirmed. That misstates the record in the opposite direction from honesty rule 1.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: All committed bills show filled-with-tick. Keep the history line as plain text ('We read Oct 2; you changed it to Oct 12 on Oct 3') and drop the hollow mark from this state. Use hollow only if a future flow lets unconfirmed reads exist as bills, which the current design forbids.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: 'Viewfinder filling the sheet on native... on iOS it wraps the system camera picker, on Android CameraX', with a Pantopus thumbnail strip, counter, privacy line and 'Add another' drawn inside that capture view. A 'camera permission denied' frame is drawn for all platforms, Android included.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: The platform document scanners (VNDocumentCameraViewController, ML Kit GmsDocumentScanner) provide auto-capture, edge detection, crop and multi-page batch, and their UI cannot be customised. ML Kit exposes only gallery import, page limit and mode. A system camera picker takes one shot with no edge detection, the exact one-shot shape v1 forbids. A custom CameraX viewfinder means re-implementing edge detection and perspective crop, heavy for a solo founder. ML Kit's scanner needs no camera permission but requires at least 1.7 GB RAM, and VisionKit exposes isSupported.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Redraw the tray as a post-capture queue. The system scanner handles shooting; the tray (over Mail Day) shows the returned pages with upload rings, delete, retake (reopens the scanner), 'Same letter as previous', the audience line, 'Scan more' and 'Done (N)'. Replace the Android permission-denied frame with a 'scanner unavailable on this device' frame that falls back to Photo Picker or a single camera shot. Keep permission-denied for iOS and web.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: Each thumbnail carries 'its own small delete control and a "Retake" affordance on long-press/hover'.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: Apple HIG: a custom gesture must be 'Not the only way to perform an important action', and buttons need at least a 44x44 pt hit region. Android recommends 48x48 dp. WCAG 2.5.8 sets a 24x24 CSS px minimum. A small delete glyph on a thumbnail that also carries a progress ring invites mis-taps on a destructive control.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Tapping a thumbnail selects it and reveals a visible action row (Retake · Delete · Same letter as previous) with 44 pt / 48 dp targets. Long-press and hover are shortcuts only. A deleted shot disappears with an Undo, not a dialog.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: The always-visible privacy line reads 'Photos are stored privately to your home and never shown to neighbors.'
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: The real exposure of a photographed bank statement is inside the household. Zeng & Roesner found multi-user homes lack access control and have tensions even when non-adversarial. Apple HIG asks for transparency about how data is used. House honesty rule 2 requires every surface to say 'Only you' or 'your household'. The line names neither the audience nor the members.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: 'Only your household can see these photos: you and Sam.' If finance permissions differ, say so here and on the privacy card, as in the next entry.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: Second explainer line: 'Everyone in this household can see them: you and Sam Reyes.'
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: f10-mail-piece-photo and f10-mail-day-triage specify that a member without finance.view cannot open a bill photo or see its amount. A blanket 'everyone can see them' is then inaccurate, and transparency guidance (Apple HIG; Zeng & Roesner on household access control) calls for an exact statement of who sees what.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: State the audience per permission: 'You and Sam can see these photos. Members without money access see that a piece arrived, not the photo or the amount.' Draw a variant frame where a member lacks finance.view.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: State 1, 'Photos kept — the default, toggle on': the photo is kept indefinitely unless the user turns the toggle off or deletes it.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: Privacy by default (GDPR Art. 25(2)) covers 'the period of their storage'. The FTC says keep only what you need, don't keep account numbers without a business need, and set how long to keep data. The photos hold full account numbers. The pilot is in the US, so GDPR is not binding, but the principle is the recognised standard.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Product call. Either make retention bounded by default (keep until the bill is paid plus N days, or N days; show it in the count line, e.g. '… kept 90 days, then deleted', where 90 is a placeholder) or default the toggle to OFF. f10-bill-provenance's 'photo deleted, bill kept' state already handles the result. Whichever is chosen, the consequence line must state the time limit.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: The newest reviewed row reads 'Comcast · Recycled · Undo (4s)' with a live countdown.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1: a time limit set by content must be possible to turn off, adjust to at least 10x, or extend with at least 20 seconds' warning, unless it exceeds 20 hours. A visible 4-second countdown on the recovery path pressures people and fails screen-reader and motor-impaired users. v1 also lists per-item Undo and 'Undo all 6', so the countdown is unnecessary.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Remove the countdown. Every reviewed row keeps its Undo until 'Finish day' (which also meets the over-20-hours exception). A transient snackbar may echo the action but is not the only path back.

contradictionsWithV1.v1Decision: Rejected-file examples: 'IMG_4417.HEIC is 31.4 MB — mail snaps have to be under 25 MB' and 'statement.pdf isn't a photo — take a picture of the page instead'. The web desktop drop target reads 'Drag photos here, or choose files'.
contradictionsWithV1.researchSays: Only Safari 17+ displays HEIC (caniuse), so HEIC uploads need conversion before web thumbnails render, and typical iPhone HEIC photos are rarely anywhere near 31 MB (a realism note, not a sourced figure). On desktop the capture attribute falls back to a file picker (MDN), which is where people drag e-bill PDFs. Scanner apps and ML Kit commonly produce PDFs.
contradictionsWithV1.recommendation: Moderate. Keep the specific-reason pattern, but make the examples realistic: an oversized ProRAW or scan file for the size case. Either accept single-page PDFs on web (render them server-side) or change the PDF copy to a constructive fix that fits a desktop user ('PDF bills aren't supported yet — add the due date by hand instead', linking to the Date sheet). Convert HEIC to JPEG before any web thumbnail.

numbers: Hit regions: at least 44x44 pt on iOS (Apple HIG Buttons), 48x48 dp on Android (Android accessibility guide), 24x24 CSS px minimum on web (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8). Applies to thumbnail delete, retake and join controls.

ML Kit Document Scanner: Android API 21+ and at least 1.7 GB device RAM (below that, MlKitException). No camera permission. Three modes (BASE, BASE_WITH_FILTER, FULL). Configurable page limit, gallery import, and JPEG and/or PDF output.
VisionKit VNDocumentCameraViewController.isSupported returns false on unsupported hardware, so plan a fallback frame. VisionKit's DataScannerViewController requires the NSCameraUsageDescription key.

Android Photo Picker: no runtime permission. Android 11+ natively, backported to Android 4.4–10 via Google Play services. Multi-select capped by getPickImagesMaxLimit(). An app can hold at most 5,000 media grants.
HEIC/HEIF displays only in Safari 17+. Chrome, Firefox and Edge: no support (caniuse).

Bias in the Loop (N=2,784, randomised): requiring a typed correction led to significantly fewer corrections and more undercorrections. Overall accuracy was 68% vs 66% (p=0.028). Reviewers corrected digit-swap errors 82% of the time and wrong-cell errors (right value, wrong year or scope) about 77%. Errors needing understanding of the rules: 31%. A technically correct but conceptually tricky table: 21%. Financial incentives had no effect.
Visual checking left roughly 30x as many errors as double entry and was no more accurate than single entry (Barchard lab, UNLV).
Frontiers automation-bias study (N=93): an error-awareness instruction raised checking effort (d = 0.67) but not correct decisions (about 4.2 of 5 correct in all groups).
Microsoft Content Understanding's utility-bill example: billing address confidence 0.96, amount due 0.52. The money field was the one routed to human review.
Nutrient example: a $6,500 value returned at 97% confidence from the wrong table column.

Vendor-reported (weak): LandingAI cites a 40–60% cut in manual review time from confidence routing plus bounding-box grounding. Mindee's example sends extractions above 95% confidence straight through.
WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1: a time limit must be possible to turn off, adjust to at least 10x the default, or extend with at least 20 seconds' warning. Exempt if longer than 20 hours. Applies to undo windows.
WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.4: actions with financial effects, or that modify or delete user data, must be Reversible, Checked or Confirmed.

USPS Informed Delivery: grayscale images of the address side of letter and flat mail, usually emailed by 9 AM, and not every piece appears (Lob summary). Per search results only, the first 10 images appear in the email and the rest on the dashboard.
Microsoft Lens: retired January 9, 2026, removed from the stores February 9, 2026, backend scanning off March 9, 2026 (Microsoft support page via search results). Don't cite Lens as a live exemplar.

topic: household-sharing: shared household spaces, invitations, roles, member rosters, household activity notifications, shared bills, and the 'Just me' path

principles.principle: Before anyone accepts, show them what they will get as a short list of plain verbs. Show the sender that same list at the moment they pick a role.
principles.evidence: Google Home: people who are invited open the invitation from the app's Inbox, review permissions, then tap 'Agree & join'. The help page tells them to 'Review what's shared when you join a home'. Admin is described as for 'trusted partners or people who co-manage the home with you', and the optional Member toggles are written as sentences ('Allowed to check device history, like camera and lock history'). Ring lists what each shared-user level can do. Limited: Live View, Event History and notifications. Standard adds Device Control and Share Recorded Video. Advanced adds device settings, user management, and adding or removing devices. Apple Home describes each of its two roles in one sentence. Resident: 'local and optional remote access to all accessories in the home at any time'. Guest: 'local-only access to specific doors, locks... on a set schedule'. Its toggles are also sentences ('Turn on to allow users to...'). Life360's support text, seen only as a search snippet because the page returned 403 when fetched, says invitees are shown a preview of the other members and then accept or decline.
principles.implication: Composer: put a one-line capability caption under each role chip. Example for Member: 'Sees and edits the calendar, sees bills and who paid, sees who lives here'. Example for Guest: 'Same as Member until Oct 1, 2026'. The manifest's 'Role offered' row expands to the same grant list the invitee will read on f3b, generated from one shared string so the two can never disagree. Roster: each role group label (OWNER / ADMIN / MEMBERS / GUEST) gets a quiet 'What can members do?' disclosure that opens that list, not a permission matrix.
principles.strength: moderate (several first-party products agree; no controlled study)

principles.principle: Name each permission as something the person can do, in plain words. Use internal product names only as a label after the verb.
principles.evidence: NN/g: even highly educated readers want succinct, scannable text and get frustrated by unexplained jargon. The article advises keeping sentences under 15-20 words. The platform exemplars describe permissions as actions, for example Apple Home's 'control your accessories from any location' and Google Home's 'check device history'.
principles.implication: On the f3b locked column and in every f3b locked-action row, lead each line with a verb a newcomer understands. Examples: 'Message your neighbors', 'Get a residency letter', 'Share what you pay in rent (Real Rent)', 'Earn a Block Founder rank'. Never show a bare product name as the whole row. Keep each row under about 6 words before the parenthesis so both columns stay scannable.

principles.principle: Give received invitations a permanent place to live. A push, email or banner is the alert; the durable list is where people decide.
principles.evidence: Apple Family Sharing: invitees can answer from the message, or later under Settings > [your name] > Invitations. Apple Home: Home Settings > Invitations > View > Accept. Google Home: an Inbox inside the app. Ring: a 'Pending Invites' section. On Splitwise's feedback forum, users asked that invite notifications open the specific group rather than the home page. Splitwise replied that its 'added to a group' email already works that way, and a later commenter said mobile notification links still sent people to the browser.
principles.implication: The f3-invite-banner 'Review' action goes to f3b when there is one invitation. When there are several, it goes to a durable 'Invitations waiting for you' list: rows on My Homes / Your places showing inviter, home, role and expiry, one row per invitation. The design doc already specifies this list, but no v1 prompt draws it. The 'new invitation' push always opens the specific invitation, never the dashboard.
principles.strength: strong (all the platform exemplars do this)

principles.principle: Keep invitation expiry short and visible to both sides. Re-sending is one tap on the sender's row. A dead link gets its own specific state, not a generic error.
principles.evidence: Apple Family Sharing invitations expire after 15 days, and Apple keeps no record of expired ones. Ring's current shared-user page says an invitation 'is valid for 14 days' and can be resent. Another Ring page in search results said 7 days, so the figure has changed over time. Ring also warns that 'Old or expired invite links will not work and can cause confusion' and tells invitees to delete old invite emails. 1Password Families: 'Invitations expire after 5 days. You can resend an invitation at any time.' Life360 codes expire after 72 hours (search snippet only). Slack invitations and invite links expire after 30 days, and admins can resend, extend or delete pending invitations and deactivate or renew links.
principles.implication: Each pending row in the roster shows 'Expires Sep 23' as text plus an inline Resend. Its overflow holds Cancel invitation (and Extend, if the backend supports it). f3b draws expired, revoked, already-used and policy-changed as four separate frames. Each names the inviter and gives one next step, e.g. 'This invitation expired Sep 25. Ask Sam Ortega to send a new one.' The composer manifest always shows the expiry date.

principles.principle: Limit open invitation links by use count, lifetime or owner approval rather than by a request in the copy. Show the exposure warning at the moment the person chooses the link (v1 already does).
principles.evidence: 1Password Families makes the organizer confirm each new member after they accept, either from an emailed link or with a 'Confirm' button beside the name. Life360 join codes expire in 72 hours (snippet). Discord's invite links default to 7 days, and the creator can set a duration from 1 minute to 7 days (or never) and a maximum number of uses (snippet; the page returned 403 when fetched). Slack links last 30 days, the owner can shorten that to 1 or 7 days, and admins can deactivate a link at any time.
principles.implication: In the composer's 'Share instead' path, state the real constraint in the manifest: 'Works once', or a shorter expiry. If the link stays multi-use, add an owner step: whoever joins by link appears in the roster's pending group as 'Waiting for your OK' with Approve / Remove, and sees no calendar or bills until approved. An active link also appears as its own pending row with 'Turn off link'.

principles.principle: Make declining cheap and final. Both sides should know what happened, and the sender should not be prompted to nag.
principles.evidence: Google Home, Ring and Life360 all put Decline next to Accept. For Family Sharing invitations sent through Messages, Apple keeps a declined invitation's record for 30 days so the organizer and the invitee both see it was declined. NN/g says to use confirmation dialogs only for actions with serious consequences, because overused dialogs stop being read.
principles.implication: On f3b, Decline is a full-size secondary button with no 'Are you sure?' dialog. The declined frame says what the sender will see, e.g. 'Declined. Sam Ortega will see that this invitation was declined.', and offers 'Back to your place'. In the roster's pending group, a declined invitation shows 'Declined - Sep 15' with Remove only: no Resend, and no reminder to the sender.

principles.principle: Before acceptance, describe who lives in the household by count, not by name, because an invitation link can be forwarded.
principles.evidence: Life360 shows a preview of members before accepting (snippet), but its codes last only 72 hours. Apple Family Sharing shows each member's name, account and role only inside the group. Freed et al. (CHI 2018, 89 participants) found that people who abuse intimate partners mostly use ordinary features of standard apps to monitor and harass, not advanced hacking. This principle is my inference from those sources, not a tested finding.
principles.implication: The f3b offer frame shows 'Sam Ortega and 2 others live here' (inviter's name plus a count). Full names and roles appear only after acceptance, in the accepted frame's 'who lives here' row. This matches the f3-household-block wording 'You and 2 others live here'.

principles.principle: Notifications about what co-residents did should be quiet and batched by default, with the person's name first. Interrupt only when the event changes what the recipient should do.
principles.evidence: Zeng and Roesner (USENIX Security 2019) ran a month-long in-home study with 7 households and 19 participants. Participants found activity notifications most useful for home security and for confirming automations. Some found them 'annoying and overwhelming', one simply did not care when other people used devices, and a single front-door entry produced four notifications. Participants were 'generally indifferent' to the transparency these notifications gave, and none reported a privacy effect. NN/g: 'If you have more than five notifications that you need to send at once, combine them into a single message', and don't notify 'for every little thing'. Apple: 'Avoid sending multiple notifications for the same thing'. Apple defines Passive as 'information people can view at their leisure', and people can choose scheduled summary delivery. Android groups four or more notifications automatically; its docs say to update an existing notification when separate notifications aren't individually useful.
principles.implication: 'Household activity' is always in-app. Its push is Passive on iOS and Medium importance (no sound) on Android by default. Events for the same home within a short window merge into one notification that is updated in place ('Sam paid 3 bills'), not stacked. bill_paid is louder (Active / default importance) only for members who still see that bill as unpaid and due soon. task_completed goes only to the person who created or was assigned the task. home_event_created stays quiet. Settings show each channel's delivery level in words ('Quiet - shows in your list, no sound').
principles.strength: strong for batching; moderate for the specific defaults

principles.principle: Push titles: at most 30 characters, the person's name first, the object early. Any caveat must be in the part that survives truncation. Keep money and street names off the lock screen by default.
principles.evidence: Android's notification design guide: the content title should not exceed 30 characters and the content text 40; don't repeat the app name; use a circular large icon when the notification is about a person. Apple: 'Avoid including sensitive, personal, or confidential information in a notification... private information that could be visible to others'; prefer brief titles; leave out the app name. NN/g's transactional-notification article notes a 240-character push limit and says the headline should summarize the message.
principles.implication: Example titles: 'Sam marked Clark PUD paid' (25 characters), 'Unconfirmed: pickup tomorrow' (28), 'Dana added Chimney sweep' (24). Body: 'Due Sep 20 - Maple St', with the amount shown in-app only. Where the user has named the home, the push uses that nickname rather than the street. Push avatars are circular initials. Keep the actor's name in the title rather than a generic 'Bill paid', because co-residents act on who did it.

principles.principle: Attribute every shared change to a named person, persistently, on the object itself. Every notification opens that exact object.
principles.evidence: Android: 'When the user taps a notification, your app must display UI that relates directly to that notification and lets the user take immediate action.' Android also says to use a person's image as the large icon for notifications from a person. Splitwise users asked for invite notifications to open the specific group. Zeng and Roesner note that their prototype could not attribute events to an automation versus a person because the SmartThings API did not expose it.
principles.implication: 'Paid by Sam - Sep 15' on the bills-list row and bill detail is the lasting record behind the push, and must never truncate before the name (v1 already says this). The wording is 'marked paid', not 'paid', because the app records the claim, not the money moving. When an attribution names someone who has since left the home, it stays and reads 'Sam (no longer here)'.

principles.principle: Actions that notify the whole household get an Undo, not a confirmation dialog, and the notification waits until the undo window closes.
principles.evidence: NN/g: use confirmation dialogs 'before committing to actions with serious consequences'. Overused dialogs lose their power ('cry wolf'), and designers should 'go to great lengths to provide undo'.
principles.implication: Mark paid (overflow on the bills list, button on bill detail) immediately shows a toast 'Marked paid - Undo'. The bill_paid fan-out is sent only after the toast closes, and an undo sends nothing. The toast is announced as a status message. The window length is a product choice; the source gives no number.

principles.principle: Once someone resolves an item, withdraw or replace the reminders about it.
principles.evidence: Apple: sending several notifications about the same thing fills Notification Center, and 'people may turn off all notifications from your app'. Android: when separate notifications aren't individually useful, update the existing notification with new information instead. Android also says not to notify for things that need no action from the user.
principles.implication: Marking a bill paid cancels that bill's scheduled reminders for every member. Any reminder already delivered is replaced by the bill_paid notice with the same thread or tag. The paid landing state on bill detail stays for race conditions only.

principles.principle: Keep roles coarse, with sensible defaults. Never show a per-person, per-capability permission matrix.
principles.evidence: Zeng and Roesner: the complexity of access controls was a barrier for novice users, and adding per-user settings took the options from 3 to 3n per device. They warn that such complexity 'risks increasing the access gap between the smart home's primary user and others with less technical or interpersonal power', and recommend sensible defaults. Google Home offers two roles plus two toggles, Apple Home two roles plus two toggles, and Ring three levels.
principles.implication: Four roles at most (Owner, Admin, Member, Guest). The composer offers only Member and Guest. No per-capability toggles in the pilot. Changing someone's role is a single overflow action on their roster row, and its sheet lists the capability difference as two short columns.

principles.principle: Show a limitation where the person would try the action, with a reason and whoever can do it. Never leave a visible control that silently does nothing.
principles.evidence: In Zeng and Roesner's study, one participant in a home with 14 devices struggled to know which devices he could use, which he couldn't, and which needed permission. Participants asked for each device's access policy to be shown on the main control page, and one household suggested simply hiding devices a person could not use. Android: a tap must lead to related UI.
principles.implication: This supports v1's lock row. Also name the person who can do the action: 'Dana or Marcus can add bills here'. The dashboard lock row, the calendar's legacy read-only caption and the bills-list caption all use the same component.

principles.principle: Design for the member who didn't set things up as a full user. The person who set up the home tends to hold most of the control.
principles.evidence: Geeng and Roesner (CHI 2019, 18 participants) observed 'an outsized role of the person who installs devices in terms of selecting, controlling, and fixing them'. They recommend designing for non-expert household members. Song et al. (CHI 2021) found that people in shared accounts can see ownership differently, one as co-owner and another as merely permitted, and that this mismatch causes conflict; they recommend making roles explicit. Zeng and Roesner found that installing the app kept some household members out entirely, and suggest a mobile-web version.
principles.implication: Invitations can be accepted fully on mobile web without installing the app (keep f3b's public variant first-class). Members get a useful dashboard. A member can record their own contribution, such as 'I paid this' on a bill. Every member can leave on their own.

principles.principle: Any member can leave on their own, and leaving or removal clearly says what they keep and what they lose.
principles.evidence: Apple Home: Home Settings > Leave Home. 1Password: an organizer can suspend or remove a member. Removed members 'lose access to all shared items' and have '30 days to sign in on 1Password.com and migrate their personal items'. Ring lets the owner remove a person from one location or delete them entirely.
principles.implication: The viewer's own roster row has 'Leave Maple St'. Its sheet lists what goes (household calendar, bills, tasks) and what stays (your saved places and your private dates). The revoked frame on the member dashboard says the same in one line under 'Your access to Maple St ended.'

principles.principle: Tell every member when someone joins or leaves, not only the managers.
principles.evidence: Apple Family Sharing: every member can see each member's name, account and role. Freed et al. show that ordinary account features are used to monitor people. Zeng and Roesner note that transparency may matter more in adversarial households than in the cooperative ones they studied. This is my inference; no study tested join notices.
principles.implication: Add a quiet in-app household row, e.g. 'Tova joined Maple St - can see the calendar and bills', and 'Jenna's guest access ended'. Keep pending invitations for managers only (v1), but when someone actually joins, every member sees it.

principles.principle: Money visibility among co-residents benefits from a per-item choice, stated on the surface.
principles.evidence: Honeydue, a couples' finance app, says 'You are in control over what you share with your partner' and offers three choices per account: balances and transactions, balances only, or nothing at all. A CHI 2025 paper on collaborative financial technologies ('In the Balance') recommends letting users adjust how visible transactions and accounts are. I saw only its abstract via search; the full text returned 403.
principles.implication: The bills-list header states the scope: 'Everyone at Maple St can see these bills'. Adding or editing a bill offers 'Visible to: Household / Only me', defaulting to Household for utilities. A personal policy such as renters insurance can be kept private. Only-me bills never send bill_paid and never appear on a member's dashboard total.

principles.principle: Treat 'Just me' as a complete, common answer, not a skipped step.
principles.evidence: US Census Bureau: in 2024 there were 38.5 million one-person households, 29% of all US households, up from 19% in 1974. NN/g says empty states should show system status, help people learn, and offer direct paths to key tasks.
principles.implication: After 'Just me', the roster empty state reads 'Just you at Maple St' with one quiet 'Invite someone' link. No re-prompt, no badge, no count of 'missing' members. Nothing in Today or the dashboard looks incomplete because the home has a single resident. This supports v1's full-size 'Just me' button and undo.
principles.strength: strong for the figure; moderate for the implication

principles.principle: Household status changes must work for assistive technology and never depend on color alone.
principles.evidence: WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.3 requires status messages to be exposed to assistive technology without moving focus. SC 2.5.8 sets a 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum target, with exceptions for spacing and inline text. Apple's default control size is 44x44 pt (28x28 minimum), and it says to 'convey information with more than color alone'. Material Design recommends 48x48dp touch targets, with about 8dp between them (search snippet).
principles.implication: Announce 'Sending', 'Invitation sent', 'Reissued', 'Marked paid - Undo' and 'You're offline' as status messages. The inline Resend on a pending roster row and Review on the banner have 44pt / 48dp hit areas even if they look like text. Expiry and overdue carry words ('Expires tomorrow', 'Overdue'), not just the warning or error color. The 6px unread dot has the accessible label 'Unread'. When a notification highlights a bills-list row, also move accessibility focus to that row or announce it, because the fading highlight is visual only.

patterns.name: Review what's shared, then join
patterns.exemplars: Google Home: the invitation arrives by email and in the app's Inbox; the invitee reviews what is shared, then taps 'Agree & join' or 'Decline'. Life360 shows the circle's members before accept or decline (support snippet).
patterns.howToApply: f3b's grant/limit columns are this pattern. Keep the header manifest (home, inviter, role, access window, expiry). In the offer state, describe other residents by count only.
patterns.pitfalls: A preview that lists members by name leaks who lives in the household to anyone holding a forwarded link.

patterns.name: Few named roles, each explained in one sentence
patterns.exemplars: Apple Home: Resident and Guest, each one sentence, plus two sentence-style toggles. Google Home: Admin ('trusted partners or people who co-manage the home') and Member, plus Activity and Settings toggles. Ring: Limited, Standard and Advanced, each with a list of what it allows.
patterns.howToApply: The composer offers Member and Guest, each with a one-line caption. The roster's role groups link to the same explanation.
patterns.pitfalls: Role names alone ('Admin', 'Member') mean different things in different products. Per-capability toggles turn into a matrix.

patterns.name: Pending invitations with resend, extend and cancel
patterns.exemplars: Slack: a Pending tab where admins resend, extend or delete invitations; an Invite links tab showing each link's creator and date, with deactivate and renew. Ring: 'Pending Invites', and Cancel Invite before re-inviting. Apple Family Sharing: Settings > Family > person > Resend Invitation.
patterns.howToApply: The roster's pending group shows sent date, expiry, Resend inline, and Cancel in the overflow. An active open link is its own row with 'Turn off link'.
patterns.pitfalls: If a new link does not invalidate the old one, old emails keep dead links around (Ring warns about exactly this).

patterns.name: Owner confirms whoever joins
patterns.exemplars: 1Password Families: after a family member accepts and sets up their account, an organizer confirms them from an email link or with the 'Confirm' button beside their name.
patterns.howToApply: Use for the open-link channel only. Someone who joins by link lands in 'Waiting for Dana's OK' and sees nothing of the household until approved. Email and username invitations skip this step.
patterns.pitfalls: Adds a wait for the joiner. The waiting state must name who approves and must not look like an error.

patterns.name: Access that ends on its own
patterns.exemplars: Ring: professional-installer access 'will automatically be removed after 48 hours unless you manually remove it sooner'. Apple Home: Guest access is limited to a schedule.
patterns.howToApply: A Guest row shows 'Access until Oct 1, 2026' (v1). On that date the row moves out of the roster automatically, and the other members get the quiet 'Jenna's guest access ended' row.
patterns.pitfalls: Silent expiry with no notice leaves the guest confused about why things vanished. Give the guest a one-line ended state.

patterns.name: Durable invitations inbox
patterns.exemplars: Apple Family Sharing: Settings > [your name] > Invitations. Apple Home: Home Settings > Invitations > View. Google Home: Inbox.
patterns.howToApply: The banner is the alert, and a My Homes / Your places 'Invitations waiting for you' list is where people decide. The banner's count line opens that list.
patterns.pitfalls: A single-slot banner with nowhere to go for multiple invitations makes people hunt for them.

patterns.name: Merge bursts into one notification that updates
patterns.exemplars: NN/g cites Instagram bundling likes into one notification. Android groups four or more notifications and asks for a summary; its docs say to update an existing notification when separate ones aren't individually useful.
patterns.howToApply: Several household events for one home within a short window become one notification that updates in place ('Sam paid 3 bills'), matching the same-day grouped row in the in-app list.
patterns.pitfalls: Android child notifications must still make sense alone, because the system can show them outside the group.

patterns.name: Choose what money you share
patterns.exemplars: Honeydue: for each connected account, share balances and transactions, balances only, or nothing.
patterns.howToApply: Each bill has 'Visible to: Household / Only me', and the bills list states its scope in the header.
patterns.pitfalls: Too many visibility levels become a settings matrix. Two choices are enough for the pilot.

patterns.name: Every member can leave on their own
patterns.exemplars: Apple Home: Leave Home. 1Password: removed members keep 30 days to move their personal items.
patterns.howToApply: The viewer's own roster row offers 'Leave this home', with a sheet listing what goes and what stays.
patterns.pitfalls: Hiding self-exit behind the owner makes members depend on the person who set up the home.

patterns.name: Notification opens the exact object
patterns.exemplars: Android design guidance requires that tapping a notification shows UI directly related to it. Splitwise users asked for invitation notifications to open the group itself.
patterns.howToApply: bill_paid opens bill detail (web route f3-bill-detail-web) or the highlighted bills-list row. A deleted object shows 'That bill was removed' with a way back (v1).
patterns.pitfalls: Landing on a generic list for an object that exists.

patterns.name: Household chore and cleaning apps (Tody, Sweepy, OurHome)
patterns.exemplars: Verifiable invite-flow details for these apps were thin. Tody sells household sync in paid tiers by household size and lets members check in to claim credit (vendor and review-site snippets). Sweepy requires premium for household sharing, and one App Store review snippet reports tasks syncing once and then stopping after a family member was added. OurHome lets families and roommates join a household with points and rewards (listing snippets). I could not verify these apps' channels, expiry or role explanations.
patterns.howToApply: Mostly a lesson in what to avoid: sync that fails silently after someone joins destroys trust in shared data. Pantopus' offline and cached states on the roster and bills should say what is stale.
patterns.pitfalls: Points and credit scoring between adults can turn a shared calendar into a scoreboard. This is inference, not tested here.

antipatterns: Adding someone to a household without an explicit accept step. Splitwise adds people identified by email or phone with no acceptance, and its help centre says the most common reason a group doesn't appear is an invite sent to a different email or phone than the account uses. In Pantopus, joining exposes calendar and bills, so f3b's accept step is mandatory.

Generic 'invalid link' errors for dead invitations. Ring says old or expired links 'will not work and can cause confusion'. Name the reason (expired, revoked, already used, rules changed) and who can send a new one.
A separate push for every co-resident action. In Zeng and Roesner's field study these were often overwhelming or ignored, and NN/g says to merge bursts of more than five.
A per-person, per-capability permission matrix. The number of settings multiplies with each person, and Zeng and Roesner warn it widens the gap between the person who set things up and everyone else.

Wording that implies watching or blaming, such as 'Priya still hasn't paid' or 'Sam hasn't opened the app in 5 days'. Zeng and Roesner found cooperative households rely on social norms more than app features, and monitoring features are the ones misused in abusive relationships (Freed et al.). This is inferred; no study tested these exact strings.
Scoreboards or leaderboards between adult co-residents. They turn shared tasks into surveillance. This is inference only; no source here tested it.
